It assembles with Bop1 and WDR12 into the PeBoW complex, which is required for processing of 32S/36S precursor rRNA into mature 28S and 5.8S rRNA; its BRCT domain is indispensable for nucleolar localization, PeBoW incorporation, and rRNA processing function, and disruption of the complex triggers p53 accumulation and cell cycle arrest [PMID:15225545, PMID:16043514, PMID:17189298]. Beyond ribosome biogenesis, PES1 directly interacts with TERT to promote telomerase RNA–TERT assembly and telomerase activity [PMID:31106266], differentially stabilizes ERα while destabilizing ERβ through CHIP-mediated ubiquitination—a process counteracted by SUMO-1/2/3 modification at K517 [PMID:22820289, PMID:27409667]—and suppresses CD8⁺ T cell–mediated immune surveillance by disrupting the ILF3–IL15 mRNA stabilization complex [PMID:36959575]. PES1 protein stability is itself regulated by Trim23-mediated ubiquitination, which is inhibited by the lncRNA SNHG17 [PMID:34782005].

PNO1 is a KH-domain RNA-binding protein essential for 18S rRNA maturation and 40S ribosomal subunit biogenesis, with additional roles in proteasome assembly and multiple oncogenic signaling pathways. In yeast and mammalian cells, PNO1 localizes to the nucleolus (via residues 92–230) and, in complex with NOB1, directs cleavage of 20S pre-rRNA to generate mature 18S rRNA; loss of PNO1 depletes 40S/60S subunits and 80S ribosomes, reduces global translation, and triggers nucleolar stress that stabilizes p53 by blocking MDM2-mediated ubiquitination [PMID:12736301, PMID:30862720, PMID:40157618]. PNO1 is essential for early mammalian embryogenesis, as homozygous knockout in mice causes pre-compaction lethality [PMID:23029399]. PNO1 transcription is repressed by EBF1 and activated by MYC and E2F6, while its mRNA is post-transcriptionally targeted by miR-340-5p and miR-326; PNO1 also participates in proteasome assembly, and its depletion stabilizes the CDK inhibitor p27 [PMID:30862720, PMID:35870038, PMID:39414903, PMID:32483111].

POLR2A/RPB1 is the catalytic largest subunit of RNA polymerase II, responsible for transcription of all protein-coding and many non-coding genes in eukaryotes. Its C-terminal domain (CTD), composed of tandem YSPTSPS heptapeptide repeats, undergoes sequential phosphorylation at Ser5 (by CDK7/TFIIH), Ser7, and Ser2 (by CDK9/P-TEFb and CDK12) to coordinate the transcription cycle and recruit co-transcriptional mRNA processing factors — capping enzymes via Ser5-P, splicing and 3′-end processing factors, and chromatin-modifying enzymes such as Set2 via dual Ser2/Ser5-P — while elongation regulators including DSIF/Spt5, NELF, Spt6, IWS1, and RECQ5 interact directly with RPB1 to control pausing, processivity, and genome stability [PMID:9002523, PMID:10199401, PMID:26799764, PMID:34967414, PMID:21402780]. RPB1 is subject to ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation upon DNA damage through multiple E3 ligase complexes — Elongin A–Cul5–Rbx2 targeting Ser5-P RPB1, ARMC5–CUL3–RBX1, and STK19-stimulated CRL4-CSA targeting K1268 — and is stabilized by deubiquitinases including USP10; sumoylation at K1487 restrains DNA damage checkpoint signaling independently of ubiquitylation [PMID:19037258, PMID:35687106, PMID:19384408, PMID:40605431]. Recurrent somatic POLR2A mutations (p.Gln403Lys, p.Leu438_His439del) drive meningioma, and de novo heterozygous germline variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome with infantile-onset hypotonia through dominant-negative or haploinsufficiency mechanisms [PMID:27548314, PMID:31353023].

POP5 is a conserved protein subunit of both RNase P and RNase MRP ribonucleoprotein complexes that functions as a critical activator of RNA-catalyzed pre-tRNA 5'-end maturation. POP5 adopts an RRM-like α-β sandwich fold and heterodimerizes with RPP30; in solution this pair forms a (POP5·RPP30)₂ heterotetramer that, upon binding the catalytic domain of RNase P/MRP RNA, converts to 1:1 stoichiometry per holoenzyme and is solely responsible for enhancing the RNA catalyst's cleavage rate by ~60–100-fold while also promoting cleavage-site fidelity (~25-fold rescue of mis-cleavage), whereas a second protein pair (RPP21·RPP29) principally increases substrate affinity [PMID:16418270, PMID:18558617, PMID:20705647, PMID:22298511, PMID:25195671]. The C-terminal helix α4 of POP5 mediates direct contacts with the RNase P RNA catalytic core, and RPP30 assists POP5 in attaining an active conformation by shielding its hydrophobic surfaces [PMID:24120499, PMID:26152732]. In human cells, POP5 localizes to the nucleus and nucleolus, and its overexpression lengthens telomeres, indicating a functional role beyond canonical tRNA processing [PMID:11413139, PMID:38789417].

PYGM encodes myophosphorylase, the muscle-specific isoform of glycogen phosphorylase that catalyzes the rate-limiting release of glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen, initiating glycogenolysis in skeletal and cardiac muscle as well as in brain cell types [PMID:25914343, PMID:22730558]. Loss-of-function mutations cause McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V), characterized by abolished myophosphorylase activity, massive subsarcolemmal glycogen accumulation, exercise intolerance, and elevated serum creatine kinase, while a dominant missense mutation causes protein misfolding and aggregation with a gain-of-function dominant-negative mechanism distinct from classical recessive disease [PMID:25914343, PMID:32386344, PMID:31511858]. Beyond skeletal muscle, PYGM sustains cardiac energy homeostasis during ischemic injury by coupling glycogenolysis to glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and autophagic flux via Thbs1 suppression, and in the brain it supports neuronal ATP production required for synaptic plasticity and astrocyte-to-neuron lactate shuttle necessary for neuronal health in tauopathy [PMID:40988610, PMID:37537141, PMID:41700129]. PYGM additionally suppresses necroptosis signaling in retinal pigment epithelium and participates in a GSTM3–PYGM regulatory axis governing hepatic lipid metabolism [PMID:41183696, PMID:41724276].

RBM19 is a conserved, multi-RNA-recognition-domain nucleolar protein essential for 40S ribosomal subunit biogenesis and early embryonic development. Its yeast ortholog Mrd1 binds pre-rRNA at helices 27 and 28 near the central pseudoknot via RBD1-3, organizes pseudoknot formation, and is required for disruption of U3 snoRNA base-pairing in the 5′ETS during 90S pre-ribosome maturation [PMID:23193268, PMID:29373706]. In mice, RBM19 is indispensable for preimplantation development: homozygous null embryos arrest at the morula stage with defective nucleologenesis, p53 pathway activation, and apoptosis [PMID:19087264]. In cancer contexts, RBM19 functions as an RNA-binding protein that stabilizes oncogenic transcripts including SNHG21 and MALAT1, promoting tumor cell survival and chemoresistance [PMID:39730751, PMID:40774403].

RCL1 is an essential component of the small-subunit (SSU) processome that functions as a novel endonuclease in pre-rRNA processing during ribosome biogenesis. In yeast, recombinant Rcl1 directly cleaves pre-rRNA at the A2 site to separate small- and large-subunit rRNA precursors, and active-site mutations abolish this cleavage both in vitro and in vivo; however, in human cells UTP24 rather than RCL1 serves as the primary endonuclease for the equivalent cleavage, indicating species-specific division of labor [PMID:21849504, PMID:27034467]. RCL1 protein stability and nucleolar import are absolutely dependent on its interaction with the GTPase BMS1, which delivers RCL1 to pre-ribosomes in a GTP-regulated manner; loss of BMS1 binding targets RCL1 for ubiquitin–proteasome degradation [PMID:16307926, PMID:37451810]. Access of Rcl1 to its pre-rRNA substrate is gated by Rrp5, which blocks A2 cleavage until 25S rRNA domain I is transcribed, thereby coupling 40S and 60S subunit maturation [PMID:31217256].

RPF1 is a nucleolar pre-60S ribosome assembly factor that contains a sigma(70)-like RNA-binding domain and functions within the Nsa1–Rrp1–Rpf1–Mak16 (WDR74) module to stabilize the solvent-exposed face of nascent 60S particles and promote proper pre-rRNA folding and cleavage [PMID:11864606, PMID:29245012, PMID:38391939]. Cryo-EM structures of sequential early nucleolar pre-60S intermediates place RPF1 within this module as rRNA domains fold and compact from the solvent side around the polypeptide exit tunnel toward the central protuberance [PMID:29245012]. RPF1 is imported into the nucleus via Kap120 and parallel importins; loss of Kap120 or RPF1 causes nuclear accumulation of 60S subunits, and RPF1 overexpression rescues the kap120 import defect [PMID:16581791]. The Mak16–RPF1 interaction is regulated by a redox-sensitive [4Fe-4S] cluster in Mak16, providing a mechanism by which oxidative stress impairs early 60S assembly [PMID:41231949].

RPF2 is a nucleolar ribosome assembly factor that heterodimerizes with Rrs1 via its Brix domain and recruits the 5S RNP (5S rRNA, RPL5, RPL11) into pre-60S ribosomal particles, a step essential for 27SB pre-rRNA processing and large subunit maturation [PMID:17938242, PMID:26117542]. High-resolution crystal structures show the Rpf2 Brix domain is completed by Rrs1 to form two anticodon-binding-domain-like folds that directly contact 5S rRNA through a conserved arginine residue (R236 in yeast), RPL5, and the biogenesis factor Rsa4, while flexible Rrs1 C-terminal tails block 25S rRNA rotation, necessitating Rpf2–Rrs1 removal for central protuberance rearrangement and 60S export [PMID:25855814, PMID:26117542]. In human cells, RPF2/BXDC1 localizes dynamically to the nucleolus and functions as a scaffold for ribosome biogenesis, and the 5S RNP whose assembly it governs also serves as the key activator of p53 through MDM2 repression [PMID:19170763, PMID:24120868]. In colorectal cancer cells, RPF2 overexpression promotes chemotherapy resistance and EMT through a CARM1–AKT/GSK-3β axis, though the biochemical basis of this extra-ribosomal function is not yet reconstituted [PMID:37997821, PMID:39674359].

RPL10 (uL16) is an essential component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit whose internal loop governs intersubunit rotational dynamics, allosterically linking the peptidyl transferase center, tRNA binding sites, and subunit interface to regulate translation fidelity, catalysis, and late-stage 60S maturation through Nmd3 release [PMID:24214990, PMID:17761675]. High-resolution cryo-EM structures position RPL10 at the core of the large subunit near the peptidyl transferase center, consistent with its role as a dynamic regulator rather than a passive structural element [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. Loss-of-function mutations (K78E, A64V, L206M) cause X-linked microcephaly, intellectual disability, and skeletal dysplasia by perturbing translational output, while the recurrent somatic R98S mutation drives pediatric T-ALL through JAK-STAT hyper-activation via altered programmed ribosomal frameshifting and IRES-dependent BCL-2 upregulation that confers sensitivity to Venetoclax [PMID:25316788, PMID:26290468, PMID:23263491, PMID:28744013, PMID:29930300]. A testis-specific retrogene, RPL10L, compensates for RPL10 silencing during meiotic sex chromosome inactivation in spermatogenesis, and the two proteins are functionally interchangeable [PMID:28502657].

RPL10A (uL1) is a universally conserved structural component of the 60S ribosomal subunit that, beyond its core role in 80S ribosome assembly, confers translational specialization and autoregulates its own expression. Near-atomic cryo-EM structures place RPL10A at the large subunit interface, where it participates in subunit joining and rotational dynamics [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. RPL10A directly binds a conserved element in its own pre-mRNA to redirect splice-site choice toward an NMD-degraded isoform, an autoregulatory circuit whose perturbation impairs T cell development in zebrafish [PMID:26961311, PMID:32571908]. In mammals, RPL10A-containing ribosomes are dynamically regulated during embryonic stem cell differentiation and preferentially translate Wnt pathway and mesoderm-specifying mRNAs; Rpl10a loss-of-function in mice causes posterior trunk truncations and reduced paraxial mesoderm production [PMID:36123354].

RPL10A (uL1) is a universally conserved structural component of the 60S ribosomal subunit that, beyond its core role in 80S ribosome assembly, confers translational specialization and autoregulates its own expression. Near-atomic cryo-EM structures place RPL10A at the large subunit interface, where it participates in subunit joining and rotational dynamics [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. RPL10A directly binds a conserved element in its own pre-mRNA to redirect splice-site choice toward an NMD-degraded isoform, an autoregulatory circuit whose perturbation impairs T cell development in zebrafish [PMID:26961311, PMID:32571908]. In mammals, RPL10A-containing ribosomes are dynamically regulated during embryonic stem cell differentiation and preferentially translate Wnt pathway and mesoderm-specifying mRNAs; Rpl10a loss-of-function in mice causes posterior trunk truncations and reduced paraxial mesoderm production [PMID:36123354].

RPL11 is a ribosomal protein of the large subunit that functions both as a structural component of the translating ribosome and as a central extraribosomal sensor coupling ribosomal stress to p53 stabilization and c-Myc suppression. Within the ribosome, RPL11's N-terminal domain acts as a conformational switch at the GTPase-associated center, facilitating EF-G-dependent translocation and differentially modulating release factor activities, while its internal P-site loop coordinates tRNA occupancy and translational fidelity [PMID:10338213, PMID:11518530, PMID:6355097, PMID:20705654]. Upon nucleolar stress, RPL11 translocates from the nucleolus—where it is normally retained by PICT1, RRS1, and GRWD1—to the nucleoplasm, where it cooperates with RPL5 to bind MDM2 through MDM2's acidic domain and zinc fingers, inhibiting MDM2's E3 ligase activity via a post-ubiquitination mechanism and thereby stabilizing p53; this pathway is regulated by NEDDylation and SUMOylation of RPL11 [PMID:12842086, PMID:15152193, PMID:18560357, PMID:21804542, PMID:26220995, PMID:30024791]. RPL11 also directly inhibits c-Myc transcriptional activity by binding Myc Box II and blocking TRRAP recruitment, and independently recruits miRISC (Ago2, miR-24, miR-130a) to c-myc mRNA to promote its degradation, forming a negative feedback loop since RPL11 is itself a c-Myc transcriptional target [PMID:17599065, PMID:21807902, PMID:24141778].

RPL12/uL11 is a core component of the ribosomal large subunit stalk that functions as the principal recruitment hub for GTP-dependent translation factors, coupling factor binding to GTPase activation, translocation, and translational fidelity. The protein adopts a modular architecture: an N-terminal dimerization domain anchors L12 dimers to L10 on the ribosome, a flexible hinge region (residues ~35–52) is essential for productive factor engagement, and a conserved C-terminal domain directly contacts IF2, EF-Tu, EF-G, and release factors RF1/RF3 through a shared surface centered on residues K70, L80, and E82 [PMID:17070545, PMID:8419370, PMID:7932718, PMID:28342293]. Post-translational modifications—including N-acetylation that stabilizes stalk–L10 interaction under stress [PMID:18514735], arginine methylation at Arg67 by RMT2 [PMID:11856739], lysine methylation at Lys3 by Set11 [PMID:18195021], and CDK1-mediated phosphorylation of Ser38 that creates functionally specialized ribosomes during mitosis [PMID:30220558]—dynamically tune translational output. The mitochondrial paralog MRPL12 additionally exists as a free pool that directly activates the mitochondrial RNA polymerase POLRMT to stimulate mtDNA transcription independently of its ribosomal role [PMID:22003127, PMID:26586915].

RPL13 (eL13) is an integral protein of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that functions in canonical mRNA translation and possesses extraribosomal regulatory activities. Structurally resolved at near-atomic resolution within the human 80S ribosome [PMID:25901680], RPL13 is required for proper 60S–80S subunit dynamics and global translation, as patient-derived missense variants alter the 60S:80S ratio and attenuate protein synthesis [PMID:32916022]. Beyond its core ribosomal role, RPL13 selectively promotes viral IRES-driven translation by cooperating with DDX3 and eIF3 subunits to facilitate 80S assembly on viral mRNAs [PMID:31619563], and it modulates NF-κB/IFN-β innate immune signaling [PMID:34093518]. Pathogenic variants in RPL13 — clustering in an RNA-binding motif — cause spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with severe short stature, establishing it as a ribosomopathy gene essential for skeletal and cardiac development [PMID:31630789, PMID:31625562].

RPL13A is a 60S ribosomal subunit protein (uL13) that possesses a mechanistically separable extraribosomal function as a phosphorylation-dependent translational silencer central to innate immune resolution. Upon IFN-γ stimulation or viral infection, the entire cellular pool of L13a is phosphorylated via the DAPK1-ZIPK kinase axis, released from the ribosome—where GAPDH acts as a chaperone preventing its proteasomal degradation—and assembles into the GAIT (or VAIT) ribonucleoprotein complex that binds GAIT-element hairpins in target mRNA 3′-UTRs and represses their translation by blocking 48S ribosomal complex assembly through direct interaction with eIF4G [PMID:14567916, PMID:17218275, PMID:22771119, PMID:24899178]. Ribosomal incorporation requires Arg68-dependent rRNA binding in the nucleolar 90S preribosome, whereas the eukaryote-specific C-terminal extension (Arg169-Lys171) is essential for GAIT-mediated translational silencing but dispensable for ribosomal function, and L13a depletion reduces rRNA methylation and IRES-dependent translation without affecting global translation or cell growth [PMID:23689135, PMID:31308261, PMID:17921318]. Myeloid-specific L13a knockout mice exhibit unresolved inflammation, enhanced susceptibility to endotoxemia, colitis, and atherosclerosis, and altered macrophage polarization, establishing L13a-dependent translational control as a critical physiological brake on inflammatory gene expression [PMID:23460747, PMID:26166763, PMID:24436370, PMID:40631353].

RPL14 (eL14) is an essential structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that assembles into pre-60S particles at an early nucleolar stage, where it is required for processing of 27SA2/27SA3 pre-rRNAs to 27SB and for subsequent nuclear export of pre-60S intermediates [PMID:29788267]. Structurally, RPL14 adopts a five-stranded beta-barrel fold with two rRNA-binding surfaces and a hydrophobic protein-interaction patch that mediates contact with neighboring protein L19, and its eukaryote-specific C-terminal extension functionally cooperates with that of L16 to influence translation [PMID:8805509, PMID:29788267]. Haploinsufficiency of RPL14 produces the classic Minute phenotype in Drosophila, while complete depletion is lethal, underscoring its essential role in ribosome biogenesis and cell viability [PMID:9236770, PMID:14597387]. PRMT5-mediated symmetric dimethylation of RPL14 at arginine residues stabilizes the protein and promotes DNA damage repair, linking ribosomal protein modification to genotoxic stress responses in cancer cells [PMID:40115921].

RPL15 (eL15) is a structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that binds a conserved site in domain II of large rRNA—requiring a partially assembled ribosomal particle—and forms a complex with acidic ribosomal proteins to organize the subunit architecture [PMID:3309345, PMID:9878356, PMID:25901680]. RPL15 is essential for pre-rRNA ITS1 cleavage and pre-60S subunit biogenesis in the nucleolus; its loss causes ribosomal stress that activates p53 via increased RPL5/RPL11–MDM2 association, leading to cell cycle arrest or apoptosis depending on cell context [PMID:23812780, PMID:35410346, PMID:31523176]. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RPL15 cause Diamond–Blackfan anemia through defective 60S formation, impaired erythroid differentiation, and TP53-dependent apoptosis [PMID:23812780, PMID:29599205]. RPL15 is a direct binding target of topotecan; its depletion or targeted degradation triggers DAMP secretion and cGAS–STING-dependent antitumor immune activation independently of topoisomerase I [PMID:35725272, PMID:41276688].

RPL17 (uL22) is a core structural protein of the 60S ribosomal subunit whose internal loop lines the middle region of the ribosomal exit tunnel, where it contacts nascent transmembrane segments in their α-helical conformation and communicates folding status to the ER translocon [PMID:21949410, PMID:24072706, PMID:23636399]. RPL17 binds 35S pre-rRNA early in 60S biogenesis, and its depletion stalls pre-60S maturation, generating translationally active ribosomes bearing a 5′-truncated 5.8SC rRNA species produced by Xrn2, thereby creating ribosome heterogeneity [PMID:9838082, PMID:25995445]. Haploinsufficiency of RPL17 causes Diamond-Blackfan anemia through impaired ribosome production, with loss-of-function variants confirmed in multigenerational pedigrees and recapitulated by zebrafish knockdown [PMID:39088281]. Beyond its ribosomal role, RPL17 suppresses vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation in vivo, facilitates HCV nucleocapsid assembly by bridging viral 3′UTR RNA and Core protein, and activates ERK/MAPK signaling in cancer contexts [PMID:23065385, PMID:38899899, PMID:35711835].

RPL18 is a core structural protein of the eukaryotic 60S large ribosomal subunit that functions in translation and additionally serves as a negative regulator of the dsRNA-activated kinase PKR by competing with dsRNA for binding to PKR's dsRNA-binding domain, thereby inhibiting PKR autophosphorylation and eIF-2α phosphorylation to maintain translational activity [PMID:9891046]. Multiple viruses—including dengue virus, Newcastle disease virus, PEDV, and rice stripe virus—co-opt RPL18 to enhance viral protein synthesis, and RPL18 knockdown selectively reduces viral translation without impairing global host translation [PMID:26092250, PMID:34859725, PMID:29374519]. Loss-of-function rpl18 mutations in zebrafish recapitulate Diamond-Blackfan anemia erythroid defects through p53 activation and aberrant JAK2-STAT3 signaling, which is rescued by pharmacological STAT3 inhibition [PMID:32075953]. In melanoma, RPL18 stabilizes BTF3 mRNA to activate STAT3 signaling, driving tumor progression, chemoresistance, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment via TGF-β-mediated M2 macrophage polarization [PMID:41550725].

RPL18A (eL20) is a core structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit, positioned in the subunit interior where it contacts neighboring proteins L4, L21, L29, and L13a and participates in subunit interface remodeling during translational elongation [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680, PMID:3988767]. Its nuclear import is mediated by importins 9a/9b, which act as cytoplasmic chaperones to shield the protein's basic domains from aggregation with polyanions before ribosome assembly [PMID:11823430]. RPL18A is phosphorylated during mitosis by cyclin B–Cdc2, linking its modification to cell-cycle progression [PMID:9115395], and it directly binds the hepatitis C virus IRES RNA to modestly stimulate cap-independent translation [PMID:16195786]. Perturbation of its C. elegans ortholog RPL-20 reduces 60S biogenesis and 80S ribosome levels, demonstrating a conserved requirement for eL20 in ribosome assembly [PMID:40691188].

RPL19 (eL19) is an essential structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that directly binds both 5S and 5.8S rRNA, forms the eukaryote-specific intersubunit bridge eB12 through its C-terminal α-helix contacting 18S rRNA, and contributes to translational fidelity at the decoding step through interactions with L14 and 16S rRNA [PMID:7400140, PMID:7251593, PMID:27038511, PMID:17157877]. Near-atomic cryo-EM structures of the human 80S ribosome confirm RPL19 at the 60S subunit interface, and mutagenesis demonstrates that its globular domain is essential for ribosome assembly while the eB12 bridge promotes subunit joining rescued by deacylated tRNA [PMID:25901680, PMID:27038511]. Beyond its core ribosomal role, RPL19 exerts extra-ribosomal functions: it modulates TLR3/ERK/IRF3 innate immune signaling in a cell-type-specific manner, activates the PERK/eIF2α unfolded protein response branch, regulates cyclin D1/D3-dependent cell cycle progression, and in HER2-amplified breast cancer drives JUN-mediated IL-4/p-STAT6 signaling that promotes trastuzumab resistance [PMID:21860608, PMID:24950402, PMID:19799608, PMID:41723529]. RPL19 protein levels are regulated by mTOR-dependent autophagy, and its depletion causes G2/M arrest and suppresses xenograft tumor growth [PMID:40771929, PMID:21799931].

RPL23 (uL14) is a core structural component of the 60S ribosomal large subunit that positions at the peptide exit tunnel, where it serves as a universal docking platform for co-translational chaperones (Trigger Factor, NAC) and targeting factors (SRP) [PMID:12226666, PMID:12702815, PMID:16316984]. Its C-tail mediates a direct physical interaction with eIF6 at the 60S subunit interface that is critical for subunit joining and is disrupted by Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome-associated eIF6 mutations [PMID:36651285]. In an extra-ribosomal capacity, RPL23 accumulates in response to ribosomal stress or oncogenic RAS signaling and binds the central acidic domain of MDM2—together with RPL5 and RPL11—to inhibit MDM2-mediated p53 ubiquitination and activate p53-dependent cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [PMID:15314173, PMID:15314174, PMID:27402081]. RPL23 additionally modulates Miz1/c-Myc-dependent transcription by controlling nucleophosmin nucleolar retention, regulates MMP9 mRNA stability via direct 3′UTR binding, and influences antigen processing and MHC-I peptide presentation [PMID:19160485, PMID:34926291, PMID:40918646].

RPL24 (eL24) is a large ribosomal subunit protein that functions as an assembly-initiator protein, binding the 5′ domain I of 23S/28S rRNA (positions ~99–107) to nucleate early rRNA folding and 50S/60S subunit biogenesis [PMID:357435, PMID:404143, PMID:3278299]. In eukaryotes, eL24 forms two intersubunit bridges (eB13 and B6) required for 60S–40S subunit joining and translation initiation, and its haploinsufficiency activates a p53–p21 checkpoint and suppresses tumorigenesis by promoting eEF2K-dependent phosphorylation of eEF2 to reduce translation elongation rates [PMID:30407570, PMID:19273598, PMID:34895463]. RPL24 depletion selectively reduces cap-dependent (eIF4E-dependent) translation of oncogenic mRNAs such as cyclin D1 and survivin [PMID:24970821]. An extra-ribosomal function has been identified in which RPL24 interacts with DDX5 to inhibit Microprocessor-mediated miRNA biogenesis [PMID:38261097].

RPL26 (uL24) is a core component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that functions at the intersection of ribosome biogenesis, translational regulation of tumor suppressors, and ER-associated co-translational quality control. As a structural subunit positioned at the inter-subunit interface, RPL26 is required for 27S/pre-rRNA maturation, 60S assembly, and normal polysome formation [PMID:18697920, PMID:22688513, PMID:23636399]; loss-of-function mutations cause Diamond–Blackfan anemia [PMID:22431104]. RPL26 acts as a stress-responsive translational activator by binding the 5′UTR of p53 mRNA (and 3′UTR of p73 mRNA), displacing the repressive nucleolin homodimer to enhance polysome loading and protein synthesis after DNA damage—an activity negatively regulated by Mdm2-driven polyubiquitylation and degradation of RPL26 [PMID:16213212, PMID:18951086, PMID:22433872, PMID:27825141]. At the ER, RPL26 is the principal substrate of UFMylation at K132/K134, a modification catalyzed by ER-tethered enzymes on translocon-bound 60S subunits that is essential for routing stalled ER nascent chains to both lysosomal and proteasomal/RQC degradation pathways, with physiological importance in erythropoiesis, Paneth cell homeostasis, and intestinal integrity [PMID:30626644, PMID:31595041, PMID:37036982, PMID:41962728].

RPL27A (uL15) is a conserved structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit, positioned near the E-site tRNA-binding region, where it participates in ribosome biogenesis, nucleolar integrity, and translational regulation [PMID:25901680, PMID:27374104]. Post-translational hydroxylation of His39 stabilizes the E-site architecture and is required for full translational activity and normal mRNA selectivity; loss of this modification shifts the translatome toward shorter, more abundant transcripts [PMID:32492015, PMID:37047141]. Reduced RPL27A expression disrupts 60S subunit maturation and activates the p53 pathway through an RPL5–MDM2-dependent nucleolar stress mechanism, producing pancytopenia, cerebellar ataxia, and impaired erythroid differentiation in vivo [PMID:21674502, PMID:27374104, PMID:32535367]. RPL27A protein stability is regulated by ubiquitination at Lys92/Lys94, which can be counteracted by the small molecule martynoside binding at the exon 4–5-encoded region, rescuing ribosome biogenesis impaired by chemotherapeutic stress [PMID:37481436].

RPL3 (uL3) is a core large ribosomal subunit protein that structurally organizes the peptidyltransferase center (PTC) through three domains—a globular hub, a central 'W-finger' extension, and an N-terminal extension—which function as a 'rocker switch' coordinating aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation, peptidyl transfer, and elongation factor binding during translation [PMID:17386264, PMID:18832371, PMID:26906928]. RPL3 is stoichiometrically methylated at a conserved histidine residue (His-243 in yeast/His-245 in humans) by the Hpm1/METTL18 methyltransferase, a modification that promotes translational fidelity, slows elongation at tyrosine codons, and ensures proteome integrity by preventing aggregation of Tyr-rich proteins [PMID:20864530, PMID:33693809, PMID:35674491]. Beyond its ribosomal role, ribosome-free RPL3 acts as an extraribosomal regulator in p53-null cancer cells, interacting with Sp1 and PARP-1 to modulate p21, CBS, E2F1/Cyclin D1, and NFκB-dependent transcription, thereby controlling cell cycle arrest, mitochondrial apoptosis, autophagy, and chemoresistance [PMID:23255119, PMID:27385096, PMID:31659203, PMID:32244996]. In cardiomyocytes, replacement of the tissue-restricted paralog RPL3L by RPL3 does not alter transcript-specific translation but instead increases ribosome–mitochondria interactions and ATP production, revealing a role for the RPL3/RPL3L switch in ribosomal subcellular localization [PMID:36882085].

RPL30 (eL30) is a core structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that also functions as an autoregulatory RNA-binding protein recognizing kink-turn motifs in its own pre-mRNA and in SECIS elements of selenoprotein mRNAs. As a ribosomal protein, RPL30 adopts an alpha/beta/alpha sandwich fold, is dispensable for 60S subunit assembly in yeast but promotes efficient translation initiation, and occupies a defined position within the metazoan 80S ribosome resolved by cryo-EM [PMID:25901680, PMID:2204809]. RPL30 represses splicing of its own transcript by binding a kink-turn in the pre-mRNA internal loop to block U2 snRNP recruitment at the branch site, and it modulates UGA-selenocysteine recoding by competing with SBP2 for SECIS element binding in a magnesium-dependent manner [PMID:18570876, PMID:15821744, PMID:23777426]. Transcription of the RPL30 gene is driven synergistically by GABP and RFX1 through a hierarchical TATA-less promoter architecture, and the protein's N-terminal region possesses conserved antimicrobial membranolytic activity [PMID:7601137, PMID:33705790].

RPL31 (eL31) is a structural protein of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that occupies a position near the polypeptide tunnel exit, where it functionally cooperates with RPL39 and the ribosome-associated chaperone complex RAC (Zuo1/Ssz1) to maintain translational fidelity and ribosome function [PMID:18829863, PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. Its C-terminal RLSR motif serves as a nucleolar localization signal required for proper nuclear and nucleolar targeting [PMID:8907615]. In cancer cell contexts, RPL31 depletion stabilizes p53 protein and activates p21/MDM2, suppressing proliferation partly through the p53 pathway, while RPL31 also promotes tumor cell growth via DEPDC1 as a downstream effector [PMID:25285958, PMID:36309731].

RPL32 (eL32) is a structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit whose expression is regulated at transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and translational levels, and whose loss triggers the ribosomal stress–p53 surveillance pathway. Transcription of the mammalian RPL32 gene is driven by a complex TATA-less promoter spanning the cap site, with functionally characterized binding sites for GABP, PEA3, YY-1/delta, TFIID, and a zinc-finger protein, as well as a stimulatory element within intron 1 [PMID:1321041, PMID:8341605, PMID:8019128, PMID:2747643]. Translation of RPL32 mRNA is controlled by the 5′ terminal oligopyrimidine (5′ TOP) motif, which sequesters mRNA in subribosomal mRNPs during quiescence and releases it to polysomes upon mitogenic stimulation coincident with eIF-4E phosphorylation; in yeast, RPL32 additionally autoregulates its own pre-mRNA splicing and translation by binding a purine-rich internal-loop RNA structure with ~10 nM affinity, and is required for 60S rRNA processing [PMID:1309750, PMID:2303467, PMID:7616567, PMID:9121443]. Depletion of RPL32 in mammalian cells impairs rRNA maturation and triggers ribosomal stress, causing RPL5 and RPL11 to sequester MDM2, thereby stabilizing p53 and inducing cell-cycle arrest [PMID:32516735].

RPL35 (uL29) is a core structural protein of the 60S ribosomal large subunit that functions in ribosome biogenesis, translational regulation, and several extra-ribosomal signaling pathways. Its eukaryote-specific C-terminal expansion segment mediates nuclear import and ribosome docking to the endoplasmic reticulum, and in yeast it is essential for 27SB-to-7S pre-rRNA processing and nucleolar release of pre-60S particles [PMID:20392820, PMID:18523488]. Beyond translation, RPL35 enhances E2F1 protein synthesis when engaged by the lncRNA lncNB1 and promotes aerobic glycolysis through an ERK/HIF1α axis in neuroblastoma [PMID:31690716, PMID:34873488], suppresses chondrocyte senescence by restraining Hedgehog/Gli1 signaling [PMID:38596341], modulates ER stress via the PERK/eIF2α pathway under stabilization by GADD45GIP1 [PMID:40604925], and acts as an antiviral effector that recruits the E3 ligase AMFR to drive K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of FMDV capsid protein VP2 [PMID:41065387].

RPL35A (eL33) is a core structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that is essential for 28S and 5.8S rRNA maturation, 60S subunit biogenesis, and normal cell proliferation; haploinsufficiency of RPL35A causes Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA), establishing that large-subunit protein defects can underlie this ribosomopathy [PMID:18535205]. Near-atomic-resolution cryo-EM structures place RPL35A within metazoan-specific ribosomal architecture at the subunit interface and tRNA-binding region [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. Beyond its canonical ribosomal role, RPL35A exerts extraribosomal functions: it confers resistance to multiple apoptotic stimuli independently of Bcl-2 family members [PMID:12175552], directly binds MYC via its N-terminal domain (residues 2–22) to drive SKP2 transcription and aerobic glycolysis [PMID:41241099], and stabilizes HSPA8 by reducing its ubiquitination [PMID:38395908]. RPL35A protein turnover is itself regulated by Smurf2-mediated K63-linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, which restrains G1/S cell-cycle progression [PMID:39871432].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: Inhibits C2CD2L/TMEM24-dependent transport of phosphatidylinositol, the precursor of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), from its site of synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell membrane (PubMed:33479206). This leads to down-regulation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway (PubMed:33479206)

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: RPL37 is an essential component of the 60S ribosomal large subunit that functions both in translation and as a stress-responsive regulator of p53 signaling. The 97–111 amino acid protein contains a conserved C2-C2 zinc finger motif and is encoded by an essential gene, as demonstrated by lethality of double-disruption in yeast [PMID:8082197, PMID:8484768]. Translation of RPL37's 5'TOP mRNA is positively regulated by CK2-mediated phosphorylation of the La protein and by the m6A reader YTHDC1 [PMID:15485924, PMID:39725796]. Upon DNA damage (UV, cisplatin), RPL37 undergoes proteasomal degradation in the nucleoplasm, triggering L11-dependent MDM2 inhibition and p53 stabilization; ectopic RPL37 directly binds MDM2, inhibits its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, stabilizes p53, induces cell cycle arrest, and downregulates MdmX [PMID:20935493, PMID:23874713].

RPL37A (eL43) is a core structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that participates in cytoplasmic translation. The protein is a small (~91–92 amino acid) polypeptide harboring a conserved C2-C2 zinc finger motif implicated in ribosomal RNA contacts, and its position within the 60S subunit has been resolved at near-atomic resolution by cryo-EM of the human 80S ribosome [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. The RPL37A gene is transcriptionally co-regulated with other ribosomal protein genes through conserved promoter elements that bind nuclear factors [PMID:8477735, PMID:8665930]. RPL37A also directly crosslinks to poly(A)+ mRNA in living cells, suggesting a potential extraribosomal role in post-transcriptional regulation [PMID:22681889].

RPL38 (eL38) is a small, lysine-rich structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that functions as a selective translational regulator of specific mRNA subsets rather than a general translation factor [PMID:33926116, PMID:15520262]. Ribosome profiling after RPL38 knockdown reveals altered translational efficiencies of ~150 mRNAs enriched for transcription regulators and Hox pathway genes, while broad transcriptomic remodeling affects p53 signaling, calcium metabolism, and osteogenesis-related programs [PMID:33926116, PMID:33675855]. Beyond its ribosomal role, RPL38 directly interacts with the m6A methyltransferase METTL3 to promote epitranscriptomic modification of SOCS2 mRNA, linking it to JAK2/STAT3 inflammatory signaling in chondrocytes [PMID:35596790]. Haploinsufficiency of Rpl38 in mice (Tail-short mutant) causes conductive hearing loss through middle ear over-ossification and chronic otitis media, rescued by Rpl38 cDNA transgene, while in Drosophila its depletion blocks spermatogonial differentiation via loss of bam expression [PMID:21062742, PMID:39187660].

RPL39 is a core component of the large (60S) ribosomal subunit that functions in the nascent polypeptide exit tunnel (NPET) to ensure translational fidelity and proper co-translational protein folding. Positioned at the exit region of the ribosomal tunnel, RPL39 directly contacts transiting nascent polypeptide chains — both hydrophobic and hydrophilic segments — and its deletion causes a ~4-fold increase in translational error frequency along with cold-sensitivity and altered ribosomal subunit ratios [PMID:10852723, PMID:24072706]. RPL39 also participates in pre-60S ribosome biogenesis during middle nucleolar stages, where it is required for proper NPET maturation and 5S ribonucleoprotein rotation, as revealed by cryo-EM and pre-rRNA processing analyses [PMID:35639884]. Loss of RPL39 reduces nascent protein synthesis and cell proliferation, phenotypes that are compensated by the paralog RPL39L, and RPL39 has been linked to cancer-promoting signaling through the iNOS pathway in breast cancer models [PMID:34428590, PMID:24876273].

RPL4 (uL4) is a universally conserved structural protein of the large ribosomal subunit whose internal loop lines the peptide exit tunnel and contacts nascent polypeptides along its entire length [PMID:24072706, PMID:25901680]. In bacteria, free L4 acts as an autogenous feedback regulator that represses translation of its S10 operon mRNA and cooperates with NusA to stimulate transcriptional attenuation via RNA-structural mimicry between the S10 leader and the 23S rRNA binding site; mutations in the tunnel-lining loop confer macrolide resistance through long-range allosteric perturbation of 23S rRNA conformation rather than direct occlusion of the antibiotic-binding site [PMID:6996835, PMID:2157208, PMID:12738792, PMID:10369764]. In eukaryotes, newly synthesized RPL4 is co-translationally captured by the dedicated chaperone Acl4, which sequesters the extended internal loop and eukaryote-specific extension to protect unassembled RPL4 from degradation and facilitate nuclear import, with RPL4 release coupled to interactions of its extension with the 60S surface including a co-evolved site on RPL18 [PMID:25936803, PMID:28148929]. In mammalian cells, RPL4 has extraribosomal functions including direct interaction with MDM2 to suppress p53 ubiquitination, interaction with RNA helicase Guα to support rRNA processing, and association with EBNA1–nucleolin complexes to support EBV episome maintenance [PMID:26908445, PMID:16045751, PMID:26858444].

RPL5 (uL18) is a core component of the 60S ribosomal subunit that serves dual roles in ribosome biogenesis and p53-dependent tumor suppression. As a ribosomal protein, RPL5 binds 5S rRNA through its N-terminal domain to form a ~7S extraribosomal RNP that is chaperoned by nucleophosmin (NPM/B23) via CRM1-dependent export for incorporation into nascent 60S subunits, and it anchors peptidyl-tRNA at the ribosomal P-site to maintain translational reading frame fidelity [PMID:3279045, PMID:16648475, PMID:11497428]. Under ribosomal biogenesis stress, RPL5 and RPL11 are mutually stabilized against proteasomal degradation, accumulate in the ribosome-free fraction, and cooperatively inhibit MDM2 E3 ubiquitin ligase activity toward p53, thereby activating p53-dependent cell cycle arrest; RPL5 additionally activates TAp73 independently of MDM2 and recruits the RISC complex to c-Myc mRNA for its degradation [PMID:23169665, PMID:15308643, PMID:25301064, PMID:24141778]. Cancer-associated somatic RPL5 mutations disrupt HDM2 binding and impair this checkpoint, and HEATR3 variants that block RPL5 nuclear import cause Diamond-Blackfan anemia-like phenotypes [PMID:32108164, PMID:35213692].

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: RPL7 (uL30) is a core structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that participates in translation as part of the 80S ribosome, with its position and interactions resolved by near-atomic cryo-EM [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. Its N-terminal bZIP-like domain mediates homodimerization and binding to both DNA and RNA, confers potent nucleic acid chaperone activity, and enables extra-ribosomal functions including coactivation of antagonist-occupied steroid receptors (ER, PR, GR) through the receptor hinge region and ligand-dependent modulation of VDR–RXR heterodimerization [PMID:8441630, PMID:8663440, PMID:9171233, PMID:9513041, PMID:27515235]. Systematic domain analysis shows that the N-terminal region harboring multiple NLS sequences is dispensable for ribosome incorporation but required for full polysome engagement, while the middle domain is essential for ribosome structure, and the C-terminal region constitutes the major autoepitope in systemic lupus erythematosus [PMID:16797011, PMID:7750987]. RPL7 also directly interacts with HIV-1 Gag via the nucleocapsid zinc fingers and cooperates with Gag in nucleic acid annealing, functioning independently of RNA binding or Gag oligomerization [PMID:27515235].

RPL7A (eL8) is an essential structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit, resolved at near-atomic resolution within the human 80S ribosome by cryo-EM [PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. The protein localizes to the nucleolus through three cooperative nuclear localization domains, with domain II (aa 52–100) necessary for nucleolar targeting, and binds RNA via two distinct domains (RNAB1, aa 52–100; RNAB2, aa 101–161), the first of which represents a novel RNA-binding motif [PMID:9030593, PMID:15361074]. Disruption of both yeast RPL7A paralogs is lethal, confirming its essentiality for ribosome biogenesis [PMID:2046660]. Beyond its canonical ribosomal function, RPL7A interacts with FKBP25 in the nucleus during oxidative stress [PMID:29969783] and promotes lung adenocarcinoma progression by forming a complex with circRANBP17 and UPF1 to destabilize SIRT6 mRNA, thereby altering lipid metabolism via the AKT pathway [PMID:41372808].

RPL8 (uL2) is an essential, deeply conserved component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that plays structural and regulatory roles in ribosome biogenesis, translation, and cell survival. RPL8 directly binds 5.8S rRNA and, following hydroxylation of its conserved His216 by the oxygenase NO66, adopts a conformation that stabilizes 28S rRNA helix 93 near the peptidyl transferase center [PMID:7251593, PMID:25702831, PMID:26327385]. The N-terminal extension of RPL8 orchestrates two sequential late nuclear remodeling steps during 60S biogenesis—ITS2 spacer removal and central protuberance rotation—by controlling the release and recruitment of specific assembly factors [PMID:27390266]. Loss-of-function variants in RPL8 cause Diamond-Blackfan anemia through impaired 60S subunit production [PMID:34961992].

RPL9 (uL6) is a core structural component of the large ribosomal subunit that functions as a molecular strut, using two RNA-binding globular domains connected by a remarkably stable nine-turn alpha-helix to brace helix 76 of 23S/28S rRNA and maintain the architecture surrounding the peptidyl transferase center [PMID:9000630, PMID:10764578]. Beyond its structural role, L9 promotes translational reading-frame fidelity by modulating mRNA movement through the ribosome—mutations in either globular domain or the connecting helix increase ribosomal bypassing, frameshifting, and stop-codon hopping [PMID:7809071, PMID:11399077, PMID:17660285]—and facilitates small ribosomal subunit maturation by reducing immature 16S rRNA accumulation [PMID:25879934]. RPL9 also exhibits extraribosomal activities including interaction with MMTV Gag in the nucleolus to promote viral assembly [PMID:23135726], binding to rabies virus phosphoprotein to antagonize viral transcription [PMID:26655239], and direct binding to HMGB1 to suppress proinflammatory DAMP signaling [PMID:35059969]. Human RPL9 variants cause Diamond-Blackfan anemia through impaired pre-rRNA processing and TP53 stabilization, while distinct missense variants instead promote stop-codon readthrough, demonstrating that different RPL9 alterations produce mechanistically divergent consequences [PMID:31799629].

RPLP0 (uL10) is the central scaffold of the eukaryotic 60S ribosomal stalk, forming a pentameric P0·(P1–P2)₂ complex that binds the GTPase-associated domain of 28S rRNA and recruits elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2 to drive translocation during protein synthesis [PMID:3323886, PMID:12060678, PMID:9988728]. The protein harbors two distinct P1–P2 dimer-binding sites (residues 199–230 and 231–258 in yeast), and its conserved C-terminal domain is phosphorylated by casein kinase II and is functionally essential when other P-family proteins are absent [PMID:16573688, PMID:1856214, PMID:7657639]. Cytoplasmic loading of RPLP0 onto pre-60S subunits requires the phosphatase Yvh1, which displaces the nuclear paralog Mrt4, establishing a regulated late step in ribosome maturation [PMID:19797078]. Beyond canonical translation, RPLP0 directly crosslinks to mRNA in vivo and interacts with ricin A chain at the ribosomal active site, and its depletion causes G1 cell-cycle arrest linked to reduced CDK2 expression [PMID:22658674, PMID:7759553, PMID:25433997].

RPLP2 is a phosphoprotein component of the ribosomal stalk on the 60S large subunit, where it assembles specifically via its conserved C-terminal domain as part of a P0–P1–P2 complex analogous to the bacterial L10–L7/L12 stalk involved in translation elongation factor recruitment [PMID:3323886, PMID:25901680]. Together with RPLP1, RPLP2 promotes efficient translation elongation through open reading frames encoding multiple transmembrane domains by relieving ribosome pausing at TMD-associated sequences, a function critical for co-translational folding and stability of multi-pass transmembrane proteins [PMID:32890404]. This specialized elongation role is exploited by flaviviruses (DENV, YFV, ZIKV), which depend on RPLP1/2 for efficient viral protein synthesis while bulk host translation is only modestly affected [PMID:27974556].

RPS10 (eS10) is a surface-exposed structural component of the 40S ribosomal small subunit that participates in ribosome biogenesis, translation quality control, and translational regulation [PMID:3378620, PMID:23636399, PMID:25901680]. It is required for the late cytoplasmic maturation step of 18S rRNA processing, and its loss-of-function mutations cause Diamond-Blackfan anemia [PMID:20116044]. PRMT5-mediated methylation of RPS10 at Arg158/Arg160 is essential for nucleolar localization via nucleophosmin/B23 interaction and efficient ribosome assembly, with unmethylated RPS10 being targeted for proteasomal degradation [PMID:20159986]. Site-specific mono-ubiquitination of RPS10 by the E3 ligase ZNF598 on collided ribosomes initiates the ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) pathway to resolve poly(A)-induced translational stalls [PMID:28065601, PMID:28132843].

RPS11 (uS17) is a conserved structural component of the small ribosomal subunit that directly contacts mRNA and P-site tRNA, functioning in translation initiation and elongation fidelity. In the 40S subunit, RPS11 occupies the platform region where it binds 18S rRNA (homologous to bacterial 16S rRNA positions 690–720 and the 790 loop) and cooperatively assembles with neighboring proteins S6 and S18 [PMID:2459389, PMID:23636399]; its direct protein–protein interaction with S7 at the E-site/mRNA exit channel is required for translational fidelity, as disruption increases frameshifting, stop-codon readthrough, and codon misreading [PMID:12937172]. RPS11 is cross-linked to mRNA in the mammalian 48S pre-initiation complex and is independently identified as a poly(A)-mRNA-binding protein by UV-crosslinking interactome capture, indicating RNA contacts beyond its canonical structural role [PMID:6514574, PMID:22658674]. Loss of RPS11 in glioma cells confers resistance to topoisomerase II poisons by impairing induction of the pro-apoptotic factor APAF1, linking RPS11 to the apoptotic response pathway [PMID:32528131].
